title: Ofgem on windless winter weeks: how safe is Britain's power supply?
label: 28 October 2026 · Ofgem on Dunkelflaute and storage
summary: Peers questioned Peter Bingham, Ofgem's engineering director, about what happens when Britain goes days with little wind or sun. He said the risk is planned for but couldn't say how rare an emergency the system is built to survive. On storage that lasts for days, the answer kept coming back to an unfinished national energy plan. He called the undersea cables to other countries reliable but not infallible, and said the real bottleneck is building the grid.

speakers.label: Peter Bingham
speakers.name: Peter Bingham
speakers.role: Director for Engineering and Technology, Ofgem

glossary.definition: German for 'dark doldrums': a spell of days or weeks with little wind and little sun, so wind farms and solar panels produce almost nothing.
The National Energy System Operator, the public body that balances Britain's electricity supply and demand minute by minute and plans for future needs.

chapters.title: How rare a blackout are we planning for?
chapters.takeaway: Unlike gas, electricity has no 'once in so many years' standard, and Lord Ashcombe struggled to get a clear answer on how bad things are allowed to get.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: Britain gets more and more of its power from wind and sun. How big a risk is that to keeping the lights on?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: It's a real issue. When wind and solar drop off, you need other power stations to fill the gap, and that takes careful planning.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: Gas is planned for a once-in-20-years winter. Is there anything like that for electricity?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: No. The target is that supply shouldn't fall short of demand for more than three hours a year, on average. NESO, which runs the grid, tests that against tens of thousands of scenarios.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: You're still not telling me what chance of the system really struggling they're prepared to accept.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: It's statistical. The aim is to cover nearly every case, but past a certain point it isn't worth the money to cover the last few.

chapters.title: Have the grid's safety rules been loosened?
chapters.takeaway: Lord Redwood asked about recent changes to the grid's technical safety rules, and Ofgem agreed to write with details.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: NESO has relaxed some of its safety limits, presumably to fit in more renewables. Could you write to us about these changes?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Yes. I know of one we approved that slightly widens the voltage range allowed, within safe limits. I'm not sure about the others.

chapters.title: Storage that lasts for days
chapters.takeaway: Peers pressed Ofgem on how Britain will store enough power to get through long calm spells, and were told much depends on a national plan that's still being written.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: To get through a Dunkelflaute we'd need storage that runs for 100 hours or more. Why is your support scheme aimed at much shorter storage?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: This first round asked for at least eight hours, and some projects reach 30. We'll consult on opening future rounds to much longer storage.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: How much storage would we need to last ten days?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The government's national energy plan should set that out. Turning it into real projects is then a job for government.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: So: lots of options, we're thinking about it, and we'll tell you next year.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: Does storage that long need a special approach from government?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Possibly. It needs huge investment and the technology is new. A separate support pot, like the one once used for tidal power, could help.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: How will you make sure it's good value for bill-payers?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: NESO is setting out options that balance cost, security and carbon. We want the Energy Secretary to pick the cheapest for consumers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Why were no hydrogen or heat storage projects chosen?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I'd need to check. The first round only accepted well-proven technologies, so newer ones were effectively shut out.

chapters.title: Relying on cables from abroad
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem says the undersea cables to other countries are reliable and aren't fully counted on in planning, but accepts they aren't infallible.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: About 15% of our power came through undersea cables last year. Why are we so reliant on them?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: They give us a bigger market and lower prices. But planning doesn't count on their full output, and we keep enough backup in Britain in case neighbours can't spare power.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Has the risk of someone deliberately cutting them been taken care of?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Every power source has a weak spot, so we plan for losing any one of them. The cables have been very reliable, but they aren't infallible.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: Does anyone check that imported power is low-carbon?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I don't believe so. Power traded in Europe doesn't come labelled with how it was made.

chapters.title: What's really holding things up
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem says the biggest obstacle isn't its own rules but how slowly the grid is being built and projects connected to it.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: What regulations are still getting in the way of building storage and low-carbon power stations?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Nothing particular comes to mind. The real problem is the grid: building it and getting projects connected. Our job is to make sure that happens quickly.
